question.prompt: A 50 mm lens is focused at 3 m. A second row is 5 m away. Comparing depth of field at the same camera position and focus distance, which single change from f/4 increases depth of field?
choices: Stop down the aperture to f/11
Switch to an 85mm lens at f/4
question.expectedAnswer: Stop down the aperture to f/11
question.explanation: Stopping down from f/4 to f/11 increases depth of field with position, focus and focal length held fixed. This is the only listed change that widens the sharp zone; it does not guarantee sharpness at both row distances.

choiceExplanations.Stop down the aperture to f/11: A higher f-number means a smaller aperture. At the fixed focus distance and focal length, stopping down increases depth of field.
choiceExplanations.Switch to an 85mm lens at f/4: At the same focus distance and f-number, switching to a longer focal length reduces depth of field rather than widening the sharp zone.
choiceExplanations.Raise ISO by 3 stops: ISO changes recorded brightness and noise behavior, not optical depth of field by itself.
choiceExplanations.Increase shutter speed to 1/1000s: Shutter time affects exposure and motion rendering; changing it alone does not increase optical depth of field.

question.prompt: An alto saxophone is an E♭ transposing instrument: its written C sounds as concert E♭. A player reads a written G major triad (G, B, D). What triad is heard at concert pitch?
question.explanation: Alto sax written C = concert E♭, so each written note sounds a major sixth lower. Written G→B♭, B→D, D→F, yielding a concert B♭ major triad.

choiceExplanations.B♭ major: Correct: transposing each note of the written G major triad down a major sixth gives B♭, D, F.
choiceExplanations.E♭ major: Written G maps to concert B♭, so the concert triad has B♭ as its root. E♭ is the concert pitch class of written C on this instrument.
choiceExplanations.F major: Moving G, B, D down a major second gives F, A, C. That is a consistent transposition, but it is not the alto saxophone's major-sixth downward transposition.
choiceExplanations.C major: Leaving the written pitches untransposed would give G major, not C major. The stated alto transposition instead gives the notes B♭, D, F.

question.prompt: For an arbitrary unsorted array of n integers, every matching index pair i < j must be explicitly listed. Can any method guarantee O(n) total time and O(n) auxiliary space for target k?
choices: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for listing every pair.
Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee O(n) total time.
Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total time.
question.expectedAnswer: No: listing all matches alone can require quadratic time.
question.explanation: If all n values and k are zero, all n(n-1)/2 index pairs match. Writing that many outputs takes quadratic time, even with efficient lookup. O(n) auxiliary storage does not remove this output-time bound.

choiceExplanations.No: listing all matches alone can requir: With n zeroes and target zero, every pair of distinct indices matches. The quadratic number of required outputs rules out a linear total-time guarantee.
choiceExplanations.Yes: a hash map guarantees O(n) time for: Fast membership checks do not avoid emitting every match. One value can match many prior indices, so total time must include the output size.
choiceExplanations.Yes: sorting and two pointers guarantee: Comparison sorting is not generally linear; more importantly, explicitly listing all matches can still require quadratic time after sorting.
choiceExplanations.Yes: nested loops guarantee O(n) total t: Checking every unordered pair makes n(n-1)/2 checks. Nested loops therefore do not guarantee linear time.
